# Honest Weight Loss Reviews — full site text

> Independent reviews of behaviour-change weight-loss apps and meal plans for adults in the United States (18+). No promises about results, no testimonials, no invented figures. Every price and trial term is checked against official pages or labelled "To be verified".

## Home

https://wlreviews.github.io/

Positioning: "Weight-loss apps, reviewed the slow way." We compare behaviour-change apps and meal plans on price, method, and fit — checking every figure against the official page before we print it. No promises about results, no before-and-after stories, no invented reviews.

What we do: compare programs side by side, including a third option; check price, trial terms, and features against official pages before publishing; say plainly who a program may suit — and who it may not; label anything unverified as "To be verified" instead of guessing.

What we don't do: promise pounds lost or a timeframe for results; publish testimonials or before-and-after stories; recommend weight-loss products to anyone under 18; write about GLP-1 medication programs or weight-loss patches.

## Hub article: WeightWatchers vs Noom — an honest comparison

https://wlreviews.github.io/ww-vs-noom.html

Status: published 2026-11-20. Full text live, about 5,350 words, 18 FAQs. Prices and trial terms checked 20 November 2026 against official pages.

Short answer: WeightWatchers and Noom are both behaviour-change programs, but they work differently. WeightWatchers is built around its Points system and workshops; Noom is built around short psychology-based lessons and food colour categories. MyFitnessPal is the third option: a tracker, not a program.

Verified prices: Noom $70 a month, or $169 for 4 months / $209 for 12 months paid up front, 7-day initial trial (checked 20 November 2026); WeightWatchers Core from $12 a month, Core+ from $20 a month (12-month plans; the Core+ offer ends 22 November 2026); MyFitnessPal Premium $9.99 a month or $49.99 a year, 7-day free trial (auto-renews unless cancelled), checked live 22 November 2026. MyFitnessPal prices changed between checks ($79.99 a year and $19.99 a month on 21 November 2026); Premium+ was not listed on the live page on 22 November 2026.

Sections: How we compare; What Noom is; What WeightWatchers is; What MyFitnessPal is, and why it is here; Price and free trial; What a typical day looks like; Who each program may suit — and who it may not; Strengths and weaknesses; Common objections, answered; Our recommendation (published, with the recommended program's weaknesses named).

Frequently asked questions: 18, covering price, trial, cancellation, exercise, food colour system, and which program fits which reader.

## Hub B: The Complete Noom Guide

https://wlreviews.github.io/noom-guide.html

Status: published 2026-11-20. Full text live, about 4,350 words, 8 FAQs. Prices checked 20 November 2026 against Noom's official pages.

Short answer: Noom is a behaviour-change weight-loss app built around daily psychology lessons, a colour-coded food system (green, yellow, orange), and a goal coach. It costs $70 a month on the shortest plan and $209 for 12 months paid up front, and every plan starts with a 7-day initial trial.

Sections: What is Noom?; How much does Noom cost? (all twelve plans, $70 to $209); How Noom works, day by day (lessons, coaching, food logging, calorie budget, weigh-ins, exercise); The food colour system: green, yellow, orange (30% / 45% / 25%); Who Noom may suit — and who it may not; Noom vs WeightWatchers and MyFitnessPal (short, links to the hub comparison); Strengths and weaknesses; Common objections, answered; Our verdict; Frequently asked questions (8); Sources.

Still to be verified (labelled in the article): Noom trial fee (if any) and whether the trial requires a card; exact cancellation steps; coach reply speed and whether coaching is one-to-one; shift-work-specific guidance.

Affiliate links: none on this page (stated in the article and footer).

## Noom vs MyFitnessPal: Behavior Change or Calorie Counting?

https://wlreviews.github.io/noom-vs-myfitnesspal.html

Status: published 2026-11-22. Full text live, about 4,310 words, 8 FAQs. Prices and trial terms checked 22 November 2026 against official pages.

Short answer: Noom and MyFitnessPal solve different problems. Noom is a behaviour-change program: daily psychology lessons, a colour-coded food system, and a goal coach, for $70 a month or $209 a year paid up front. MyFitnessPal is a calorie-counting tracker: log food with barcode or voice search, track macros, and log exercise, with a free version and Premium at $49.99 a year.

Verified prices (22 November 2026): Noom $70 a month, or $169 for 4 months / $209 for 12 months paid up front, 7-day initial trial; MyFitnessPal Premium $49.99 a year or $9.99 a month, 7-day free trial (auto-renews unless cancelled). MyFitnessPal prices changed between checks ($79.99 a year and $19.99 a month on 21 November 2026); Premium+ was not listed on the live page on 22 November 2026.

Sections: Noom vs MyFitnessPal at a glance; The core difference: behaviour change vs calorie counting; How Noom works; How MyFitnessPal works; Food tracking compared; Coaching and support; Price compared; Free trials compared; Who each one suits — and who it does not; Strengths and weaknesses; Common objections, answered; Our verdict; Frequently asked questions (8); Sources.

Still to be verified (labelled in the article): Noom trial fee (if any) and whether the trial requires a card; exact cancellation steps for Noom; coach reply speed and whether coaching is one-to-one.

Affiliate links: none on this page (stated in the article and footer).

## Can You Use Noom Without Exercise? What It Requires

https://wlreviews.github.io/noom-without-exercise.html

Status: published 2026-11-22. Full text live, about 2,512 words, 6 FAQs. Facts checked 22 November 2026 against Noom's official pages.

Short answer: Yes. Noom does not require exercise. It starts with food — exercise is something you add when you are ready, starting with 200 steps a day. There is no gym requirement, no workout plan, and no exercise target you must hit. What Noom asks of you every day is a short lesson of 5–15 minutes, logging everything you eat, and — if you want — a daily weigh-in and a check-in with your coach.

Verified facts (22 November 2026): exercise tracking starts with 200 steps a day (app includes a pedometer), building up as confidence builds; food comes first; daily lessons 5–15 minutes based on CBT; plan usually around 16 weeks; 7-day initial trial; $70 a month or $209 for 12 months paid up front; food colours green, yellow, orange; syncs with Apple Watch, Fitbit, and Garmin (plus iHealth, Misfit, Omron, Polar, Qardio, Runkeeper, Withings, Yoo); tracks weight, water intake, glucose levels, and blood pressure.

Sections: What Noom actually asks you to do every day; What Noom says about exercise; What a day without exercise looks like; When exercise does enter the picture; Who this suits — and who it may not; Common objections, answered; Our verdict; Frequently asked questions (6); Sources.

Still to be verified (labelled in the article): Noom trial fee (if any) and whether the trial requires a card; exact cancellation steps for Noom; how quickly a Noom coach replies and whether coaching is one-to-one; Noom does not publish a specific exercise target beyond starting at 200 steps a day.

Affiliate links: none on this page (stated in the article and footer).

## Noom Food Color System: Green, Yellow, and Orange Explained

https://wlreviews.github.io/noom-food-color-system.html

Status: published 2026-11-22. Full text live, about 2,543 words, 6 FAQs. Facts checked 22 November 2026 against Noom's official pages.

Short answer: Noom sorts every food you log into green, yellow, or orange by calorie density — not good or bad. Green is about 30% of daily intake, yellow about 45%, orange about 25%, and no food is off limits.

Verified facts (22 November 2026): colours are green/yellow/orange (not red); green is the least calorie-dense (most vegetables, some fruits, whole grains); yellow is the largest share (lean meats, starches, avocados, legumes); orange is the most calorie-dense and/or has the fewest nutrients (cheeseburgers, desserts); "orange doesn't mean bad"; the tracker tells you the colour when you log; suggested daily allotment for each colour; half a pound of peanut butter 1,334 calories vs half a pound of spinach 52; half a pound of oatmeal 154 calories and green because of fiber.

Sections: What the colors actually mean; Green: about 30%; Yellow: about 45%; Orange: about 25%; How the system works when you log; What the colors do not mean; Common mistakes; How this fits the rest of Noom; Our verdict; Frequently asked questions (6); Sources.

Still to be verified (labelled in the article): Noom trial fee (if any) and whether the trial requires a card; exact cancellation steps for Noom; how quickly a Noom coach replies and whether coaching is one-to-one; the official pages give examples for each color, not complete food lists — the tracker assigns the color when you log.

Affiliate links: none on this page (stated in the article and footer).

## What Is Noom Behavior Change? CBT Lessons Explained

https://wlreviews.github.io/noom-behavior-change.html

Status: published 2026-11-22. Full text live, about 2,689 words, 6 FAQs. Facts checked 22 November 2026 against Noom's official pages.

Short answer: Behavior change in Noom means changing how you think and feel about eating, not just what you eat. Daily lessons of 5–15 minutes, based on cognitive behavioral therapy, teach you to spot triggers, handle emotional and stress eating, tell genuine hunger from "head hunger," and manage plateaus. Not a fad diet, no banned foods, no pre-packaged meals.

Verified facts (22 November 2026): psychology-based approach, "weight loss isn't just about what you eat, but why you eat"; sustainable habits for a lifetime; step-by-step changes; daily lessons around 5–15 minutes from day one, with exercises, quizzes, or tasks; seven lesson topics named on Noom's page (triggers; emotional and stress eating; what to do instead of reaching for a snack; mindfulness; choosing filling foods; genuine hunger vs "head hunger"; managing plateaus); lessons based on CBT, "a type of therapy that's been proven to help people change their habits and behavior", "gold standard in behavioral science"; Noom does not believe in losing weight through sheer willpower or by restricting foods; not a fad diet or an elimination diet; plan usually around 16 weeks; 7-day initial trial; $70 a month or $209 for 12 months.

Sections: What "behavior change" means here; The daily lessons: what they actually teach; CBT, in plain terms; What a lesson looks like in a day; What behavior change does not mean; Who this suits — and who it may not; Common objections, answered; Our verdict; Frequently asked questions (6); Sources.

Still to be verified (labelled in the article): Noom trial fee (if any) and whether the trial requires a card; exact cancellation steps for Noom; how quickly a Noom coach replies and whether coaching is one-to-one; Noom does not publish the full lesson curriculum — the topics listed here are the ones named on its official pages.

Affiliate links: none on this page (stated in the article and footer).

## About and disclosure

https://wlreviews.github.io/about.html

Method: three options per comparison, same five points (price and trial terms, daily use, coaching and support, food tracking, cancelling), figures checked against official pages on the day of writing, real weaknesses listed, a second check before publishing, no star ratings.

Affiliate disclosure: Honest Weight Loss Reviews may earn a commission if you buy through a link on this site, at no extra cost to you. Commission does not change what we write.

For adults only: this site is written for adults aged 18 and over. We do not promote weight-loss products to anyone under 18.

What we don't do: promise pounds lost or a timeframe; publish testimonials or before-and-after stories; cover GLP-1 medication programs, weight-loss patches, or supplements of unknown origin; publish AI-generated content presented as a real person's experience.
